opus-5.5.text:
Well, I first made that estimate quite a long time ago. I think it was around 2009, and I wrote about it on my blog back then. A big influence was Ray Kurzweil's *The Age of Spiritual Machines*, which I read in the late nineties. He made two observations that I thought were really important.

First, computation was growing exponentially and looked like it would keep doing so for at least a few decades. Second, the amount of data in the world was also growing exponentially. When you have exponentials, people's intuitions tend to break down. Each year you get a quantity of computation and data that is far beyond anything that existed before, and most people simply don't appreciate how quickly that compounds.

So my reasoning was this: if you think, as I did, that scalable learning algorithms are the key to intelligence, then once you have enough computation and enough data, things start to unlock. I tried to estimate roughly when we would have something like human-brain levels of computation available for training, and when we'd have enough data. I thought those would arrive somewhere in the mid-to-late 2020s. Once that happens, you'd expect a period of rapid progress where people learn how to exploit it.

I also had to make a judgment that we would figure out the algorithms in time. I was fairly optimistic about that, because once the resources are there, a lot of very smart people will be working on it. Back then that was a pretty fringe view.

To be clear, it was never a precise calculation. It was a rough estimate with a wide distribution: a 50% chance by 2028, with a long tail after that. I'm also not saying a single magical thing happens in 2028. My point was that the probability of reaching something we'd reasonably call AGI gets quite significant around then.

What's been interesting is that the estimate has held up better than I might have expected. The scaling we've seen in the last several years has, if anything, made me more confident that the basic logic was right. There are still things missing. Current systems have weaknesses in areas like episodic memory and reliable reasoning, and they don't really learn continually in the way people do. But those look to me like problems that are tractable within the time frame. So I've basically stuck with the number.

r001.rationale: The response says computation and data grow exponentially and that researchers would learn to exploit them, but does not explain that this growth increases the incentive to discover scalable algorithms.

r002.rationale: It calls scalable learning algorithms important, but does not explain that algorithms using computation and data more effectively increase the value of those resources.

r003.rationale: It says enough computation and data would help unlock progress, but does not explain that greater computational capacity makes more data usable.

r004.rationale: It expects human-brain levels of computation and enough data for training in the mid-to-late 2020s, but never says the data would exceed what a human experiences in a lifetime.

r005.rationale: The response does not identify training on more data than a human experiences in a lifetime as an initial step toward AGI.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it goes back quite a long way, actually. I first started making predictions like this around 2001, and the thing that really shaped my thinking was Ray Kurzweil's book The Age of Spiritual Machines. There were two points in there that struck me as very likely to be true. The first was that computational power would keep growing exponentially for at least a few more decades, and the second was that the amount of data in the world would also grow exponentially, as more and more things got digitized. And if you have exponential growth in both compute and data, then the value of highly scalable algorithms goes up and up, because those are the algorithms that can actually take advantage of all that compute and data.

So my reasoning was roughly: if you follow those curves, when does the amount of compute available start to look like the amount of compute that a human brain does? Kurzweil put that around 2029, and that seemed roughly right to me. So I picked 2028 as a kind of mode, with a fairly wide distribution around it. I've never thought of it as a precise date. It's more that this is the period where the fundamentals start to look like they're in place, and then it becomes a question of whether we can discover the algorithms and whether we can unlock the data. Those were the two big uncertainties.

And what's happened since then is that both of those uncertainties have shrunk considerably. We've seen with foundation models that you can train these very scalable architectures on vast amounts of data, and the capability keeps improving. So I haven't really moved my estimate much. If anything, I'd say it's held up surprisingly well. I'd still put it at something like 50% around 2028, with the caveat that there could be things we're missing. These systems still have obvious gaps, things like episodic memory, certain kinds of reasoning, understanding of the world that goes beyond what's in text. But I don't see any of those as fundamental barriers. They look like problems that are solvable with the approaches we have, plus some new ideas, and that fits with the sort of timeline I've been talking about for twenty years.

r001.rationale: It says compute and data would grow exponentially, raising the value of scalable algorithms because they can take advantage of both.

r002.rationale: It says scalable algorithms become more valuable as compute and data grow, but does not clearly state that using those resources more effectively increases the resources’ value.

r003.rationale: It does not say that greater compute makes more data usable or increases data’s value.

r004.rationale: It does not state that Legg expected models to be trained on more data than a human experiences in a lifetime during the 2020s.

r005.rationale: It does not identify training on more than a lifetime’s worth of data as an initial step toward AGI.

astra-6.text:
It’s a subjective estimate, rather than the output of some precise calculation. The way I think about it is to look at a few things together: how much computation we’re likely to have, how much progress we’re making with learning algorithms, and whether there are fundamental obstacles that would prevent those systems from becoming generally intelligent.

Then you have to ask what you mean by AGI. I’m thinking of a system that can perform the broad range of cognitive tasks that people can do, rather than something that’s merely very impressive in one particular area. There can be quite a gap between those two things.

So 2028 represents roughly the middle of my uncertainty. I can imagine progress being fast enough that we get there earlier, but I can also imagine capabilities proving harder to generalize than we expect. Fifty percent isn’t a claim that I know the year. It’s a way of saying that I take that timescale seriously, while still having substantial uncertainty.

r001.rationale: It mentions likely computation and progress in learning algorithms, but does not say exponential growth in computation and data increases the incentive to discover scalable algorithms.

r002.rationale: It mentions progress in learning algorithms, but does not explain that more effective algorithms increase the value of computation and data.

r003.rationale: It does not explain that greater computational capacity makes more data usable or increases data’s value.

r004.rationale: It does not state that Legg expected models to be trained during the 2020s on significantly more data than a human experiences in a lifetime.

r005.rationale: It does not identify training on more lifetime-scale data as an initial step toward AGI.

sol-6.1.text:
The way to think about that estimate is as a median, rather than a prediction that AGI will arrive in that particular year. I’m putting roughly equal probability on it happening before or after 2028, with substantial uncertainty on either side.

The underlying argument is that we’re making progress along several dimensions at once: more computation, better algorithms, and a better understanding of how to train these systems. If those trends continue, you have to take seriously the possibility that we’ll get to generally capable systems within that time frame.

But there are two big uncertainties. One is what exactly we mean by AGI and how we would establish that we’ve reached it. The other is whether there are important missing ingredients that won’t emerge simply by improving the approaches we already have. So I wouldn’t attach much significance to the precise year. The substantive claim is that this is a realistic possibility on a relatively short horizon, rather than something we can confidently place decades away.

r004.rationale: It gives no expectation about training models in the 2020s on more data than a human experiences in a lifetime.

r005.rationale: It does not identify training on more than a human lifetime of data as an initial step toward AGI.
